title: TB9-03389
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The appellant, XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Burundi, is appealing against the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision dated January 9, 2019.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Burundi, is appealing against the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision dated January 9, 2019. Determination

The appeal is allowed. The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes the determination that, in its opinion, should have made, namely, that the appellant is a Convention refugee. Allegations

The appellant is a Tutsi who became a member of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX party on XXXX XXXX, 2013, while he was studying in Uganda. He attended seminars and recruited members among his university's student body. After he returned to Burundi, Imbonerakure militants went to his XXXX neighbourhood on XXXX XXXX, 2016, and arrested two of his XXXX colleagues. Out of fear of being arrested himself, he took steps to leave the country. According to the family of one of the detained individuals, the appellant was named under torture. On January 5, 2018, a friend told him not to go home because Imbonerakure and police officers had gone there to get him. He hid until he left the country with a Canadian visa on XXXX XXXX, 2018. Refugee Protection Division's findings

The determinative issue was credibility. The RPD rejected the claim for the following reasons:1 i) The appellant's testimony was vague regarding his political activities in Uganda. ii) No reasonable explanation was given for the fact that the original XXXX party membership card was not provided. iii) The appellant made no reasonable effort to obtain evidence of his political activities in Uganda. iv) The appellant's testimony regarding the XXXX policies and platform was vague. v) The appellant's testimony on his recruitment and fundraising work was vague. Grounds of appeal

The appellant raised the following issues: i) Did the RPD breach natural justice by failing to express the concerns on which it based itself? The RPD disregarded the letter from the XXXX president confirming the appellant's membership in the party. The RPD failed to explain why it did not believe that the appellant is a party member. ii) Is the RPD's credibility assessment unreasonable, based on incorrect plausibility findings, or unreasonable, given that the RPD did not take into account the evidence that the appellant was a member of the XXXX? iii) Did the RPD err in failing to assess the objective risk or, if the RAD should substitute a decision, does the appellant have an objective risk? As a Tutsi and XXXX member, the appellant is subjected to an objective risk. The RPD did not analyze this risk. Administrative issues
I applied the correctness standard of review. In this case, the RPD did not enjoy a meaningful advantage over the RAD.2

The appellant is requesting the admission of a piece of evidence that is described in subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and a document that was provided after the appeal record was perfected. He is also asking that a hearing be held pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.
A digital audio recording of the hearing is available, as is a transcript that is on the appeal record.
The version of the National Documentation Package (NDP) before the RPD is dated April 30, 2018. The affidavit submitted after the filing of the appeal record is not admissible

The appellant submitted an affidavit from XXXX XXXX, president of the XXXX, after the appeal record was filed. Mr. XXXX confirms that he authored the letter filed with the RPD. He was able to verify with local members that the appellant was an active party member. The appellant recruited new members among the Burundians in Uganda while he was studying there. He continues to be a member in Canada.3

The appellant asked that it be admitted under rule 37 of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules. However, he did not address the requirements set out under rule 29. Specifically, he failed to explain why the affidavit could not be obtained and submitted with the record. The RPD's decision is dated January 9, 2019, and the appeal record was submitted on February 28, 2019. The RAD received the affidavit on November 28, 2019, without any explanation for the delay other than that the document was under the control of a third party. Under subrule 29(4), the RAD must consider any relevant factors, including its relevance and probative value, what the document brings to the appeal, and whether, with reasonable effort, the document could have been provided with the appeal record. All the factors were addressed, except for the issue of efforts made to obtain it before the record was filed.

Given that the author lives in Belgium, a late filing of a few months is understandable. However, a delay of nine months without an explanation is not. The document is not admissible on grounds of non-compliance with rule 29. The letter from the XXXX representative in Canada is admissible

The appellant filed a letter from the XXXX representative in Canada on the appeal record.4 The author examined the original membership card and confirmed that it is genuine. The appellant is a party member in Toronto and began attending events shortly after his arrival.

Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA states that "the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection."5 In addition, in Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal held that credibility, relevance and newness must be taken into account.6 Evidence may be new if it is capable of contradicting a finding of fact made by the RPD, including a credibility finding.7

In this case, the appellant filed a letter of support from the XXXX president with a copy of his identity card. The original copy of the letter was submitted at the hearing. A photocopy of his membership card was also submitted. The appellant could not reasonably have expected that the original letter from the president would be disregarded and that his membership card would not be accepted as genuine. This document is admissible as new evidence because it contradicts an unanticipated negative credibility finding.

This new evidence is from a credible source, is relevant and has significant probative value because it contradicts a negative finding of fact by the RPD. Given that the document does not raise an issue with respect to the appellant's credibility, a hearing is not required pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA. ANALYSIS Political activities in Uganda

In the RPD's view, the appellant did not present any documentary evidence to corroborate his political work in Uganda. His explanation for the lack of documentary evidence was vague and evasive. He testified that he left all the documents in Uganda because they would have put him in danger in Burundi. However, this does not explain why he made no effort to obtain them after he arrived in Canada. This factor undermines his credibility. Furthermore, the university attestations from Uganda are not genuine because the stickers are different on each document. A Canadian visa application was rejected because of concerns as to the genuineness of the school records.

According to the appellant, this was a typographical error (transcripts) that did not prevent a visa from being issued in 2018 or his admission to a Canadian university. In addition, the RPD did not question the genuineness of the transcript at the hearing.

I agree that this concern should have been addressed at the hearing. Furthermore, this error has nothing to do with the seals. As the appellant notes, there are many reasons why different seals may have been used on different documents.

The appellant provided a reasonable explanation for not having brought back XXXX documents to Burundi. He took no steps to obtain them after he arrived in Canada because he was relying on the letter of attestation from the party president and his membership card. Although the appellant would have been wise to try to obtain all the relevant supporting documents, the fact that he failed to do so is not sufficiently serious, in light of all the circumstances, to justify a negative inference being drawn with respect to his credibility. XXXX membership card

The appellant had left his original XXXX membership card at home in Toronto. In the opinion of the RPD, this does not reasonably explain the absence of the original, given that he had brought the originals of the other documents and was represented by a specialized lawyer. The appellant did not ask for authorization to submit the original after the hearing. This significantly undermines his credibility.

The appellant argues that the RPD breached the principles of natural justice by failing to inform him that this was an issue that called into question the genuineness of the card. The appellant should not be expected to have read the panel's mind in order to ask that it be admitted after the hearing.

I agree with this submission. The RPD should have raised the issue in order for the appellant to know that his card would otherwise be rejected. Furthermore, the RPD disregarded the original copy of the letter from the XXXX president with his identity card. The RPD also failed to take into account the letter from the mother of the colleague who was detained on XXXX XXXX, 2016, and killed on XXXX XXXX, 2017.8 Political activities within the XXXX

The appellant claimed that he was politically active between 2013 and his departure from Burundi in 2017. In the view of the RPD, his testimony regarding the XXXX platform was vague. He was unable to explain the party's specific policies. He did not provide a reasonable explanation for how he raised funds. He was vague with respect to the number of people recruited for the party.
The appellant argues that it is unclear as to how the RPD concluded that his testimony was vague and insufficient. It also erred in assessing plausibility considering the lack of evidence.

I agree. The RPD asked several open-ended questions and received an adequate response to each of them. His responses were reasonable. If the RPD wanted more details, it should have asked. It is unfair to conclude that his testimony was vague after asking a single question on each subject, given the detailed responses that were given. Refugee Appeal Division's observations

I listened to the audio recording and read the transcript. The appellant's responses were spontaneous and reasonably detailed. His testimony was consistent and supported by letters from the XXXX president and his colleague's mother. Furthermore, the attestation of the XXXX representative in Canada confirms his membership in the party. The RPD did not justify its rejection of his testimony or the genuineness of the supporting evidence. The RPD also disregarded important evidence without explanation. My independent assessment leads me to find that the appellant is credible and that the evidence on the record is likely genuine.

The appellant presented a summary of the political situation in Burundi.9 Specifically, a Response to Information Request concerning the treatment of XXXX members establishes an objective basis for his subjective fear.10 For example, Human Rights Watch states that "'[s]cores of opposition party members have been arrested, ill-treated, and illegally detained, and other detainees taken to unknown destinations,' yet arrest warrants were almost never produced by the police." The fact that he is an ethnic Tutsi is an aggravating factor. There is a serious possibility that the appellant would be arrested and seriously ill-treated to the point of persecution.

Given that the agents of persecution represent the government, state protection is not available and the risk is present throughout the country. There is a nexus between his situation and the definition of a Convention refugee on the ground of political opinion. The appellant has a well-founded fear of persecution.

The appellant tried to raise the issue of persecution based on his Tutsi ethnicity separately from his political activities. The appellant does not mention this risk in his Basis of Claim Form and it was not raised at the hearing. The RPD did not err on this issue. Given that this issue could reasonably be expected to have been raised at the hearing, it is not new for the purposes of the appeal. This submission is rejected.

The appeal is allowed. Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the IRPA, the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes the determination that, in its opinion, should have been made, namely, that the appellant is a Convention refugee.
